To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Fake blue pills: if someone goes down, ring 999 straight away. Parents and teenagers, please read

If you're with someone who's taken something and they go down, ring 999 straight away. Don't put them to bed to sleep it off, and don't hold off because you're scared of getting in trouble. If you only read this far, that's the bit I need parents and teenagers to take in.

The police warning Gaz shared on Friday has got lost under everything else, so here it is again. Blue tablets are being sold in south Manchester as diazepam or "Xanax". They're fakes. Some have been found to contain nitazenes, which are synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin.

The signs to look for:
- extreme drowsiness, can't be woken properly
- pinpoint pupils (the black bit of the eye gone tiny, like a pinprick)
- slow or noisy breathing
- blue lips

I'm a nurse, and this next bit is general. It isn't about any one person or any one night. What happens again and again is that mates panic. They put the person in bed to sleep it off and ring hours later when they can't wake them. By then the brain has been without oxygen for too long. Ringing early is what makes the difference.

To the teenagers reading this, or having it read out at you: the police have put it in writing, "Our priority is preserving life." The ambulance is coming to help your mate, not to tell you off. Ring, and stay with them until help gets there.

I'm not going to say anything about Saturday. Nadia's already asked people not to guess and she's right. But slagging the kids off helps no one. Scared kids don't ring for help, and that is the whole problem. If we want them to pick up the phone, they need to know the adults round here will back them for doing it.

One more useful thing. Naloxone is a nasal spray that reverses opioids. You can get a kit free from Brightpath, the drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette. Anyone can ask and they don't need your name. They show you how to use it and it takes about 10 minutes. They're open Monday to Friday 10 till 4, and till 7 on Thursdays. If you ever do use it on someone, you still ring 999.

Two things I'm asking:

1. Parents, talk to your kids this week. Not when it's all died down, not whenever it next comes up. I had the chat with my lad last night over his tea. He's 14, there were eye rolls, but he listened, and he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. That's all it needs to be: ten minutes, what the tablets are, what the signs are, and that if a mate goes down they ring 999 and they will not be in trouble with you for it.

2. Please share this, don't just like it. A like doesn't put it in front of the parent who hasn't seen it, or the kid who needs to.

Becky
